proxy_language: Middle Persian (Pahlavi, Sasanian-era Zoroastrian court language), with Avestan used for sacral/divine terms
proxy_rationale: 'Light-and-Flame Court' in Iran/Persia at a later period index strongly suggests a Sasanian-style Zoroastrian fire-temple court (atash/ataxsh, roshan). Middle Persian is well attested (inscriptions, Book Pahlavi, Manichaean and Psalter texts) and is the best proxy; Avestan supplies religious vocabulary. The culture is a game construct, so the link to any specific historical court is loose.
phonology: Middle Persian consonants: p b t d k g c j (affricates, written c, j), f s z sh (š) zh (ž) x (voiceless velar fricative) h, m n, r l, y w; gamma and theta/delta only as allophones or in Avestan. Vowels: a ā i ī u ū e ē o ō (long/short contrast; e/o mostly long in later Middle Persian). Avestan adds θ δ γ and many more vowels (ə, ą etc.).
phonotactics: Syllables (C)V(C)(C); no initial clusters in native words (Old Persian clusters like *sp- developed prothetic vowels: spah > sipah; *star > istar), so word-initial st-, sp-, sr- are avoided and given a prothetic i- (ist-, isp-). Final clusters are allowed (-st, -nd, -rd, -xt, -ft, -rz). Many words end in a consonant; final -ag/-ig/-ōg adjectival and agentive suffixes are common. Stress is not marked in transliteration.
orthography: Scholarly Latin transliteration of Book Pahlavi: a ā b c d e f g h i ī j k l m n o ō p r s š t u ū w x y z ž; long vowels written with macron (ā ī ū ē ō). Plain ASCII versions (sh, zh, ch for c, kh or x for x) are acceptable in a game: sh for š, zh for ž, j, ch for c.
morphology: Little inflection: nouns have a singular/plural opposition (-ān for animates, -īhā/-ihā for others), no grammatical gender and no case in later Middle Persian (the oblique case is only remnant). Ezafe particle -ī (-ē/-ī) links head to modifier/genitive. Adjectives follow the noun. Abstract nouns in -īh (-ih), agent nouns in -ag/-ōg/-gar/-bān/-bed, adjectives in -ig/-ag/-ōmand/-ēn, place nouns in -stān/-gāh/-dān (e.g. -gāh 'place', -stān 'land of', -dān 'container'). Verb stems: present stem and past stem, infinitives in -tan/-dan, e.g. kardan, dādan, dīdan.
compounding: Head-final determinative compounds (modifier + head): ātaxš-gāh 'fire-place', dar-bān 'door-keeper'. Ezafe construction head + -ī + modifier for 'X of Y': ātaxš ī wahrām 'Fire of Victory' (Bahram fire); dar ī xwadāy 'court of the lord'. Possessive/agentive compounds with -bān 'guardian', -bed 'master/chief' (mowbed 'chief priest'), -gar 'maker', -dār 'holder', -wēnēd. Numerals and adjectives precede nouns only in compounds; independent adjectives follow with ezafe.
noun_phrase_order: Head noun first, then ezafe -ī, then modifier(s): dar-ī rōšn 'bright court' (or rōšn dar in compound/adjective-first marked usage); genitive after head: ātaxš ī xwarrah 'fire of glory'. Demonstratives and numerals precede the noun; adjectives follow with ezafe.
sources: Skjærvø, Introduction to Zoroastrianism and Middle Persian materials (2006)
Brunner, 'Middle Persian' in Compendium Linguarum Iranicarum (1989)
Durkin-Meisterernst, Dictionary of Manichaean Middle and New Persian (2004)
Wiktionary Middle Persian entries and Proto-Iranian reconstruction pages
Glottolog and Starling Iranian etymological database
notes: No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word. Use Middle Persian forms with ezafe -ī for 'X of Y'. Avoid initial consonant clusters. The earlier game strings (Ruxih ya yuvxu etc.) do not resemble Middle Persian and should be replaced.
